title: Job 39:1–18
context: The LORD continues his first speech to Job from the whirlwind, begun in Job 38:1, and the whole of this unit is the LORD’s speech. Having asked about the earth, sea, sky, and the lion and raven (Job 38:39–41), he now turns to wild creatures that live beyond human control: mountain goats and does giving birth unseen, the wild donkey roaming the salt land free of the city and the driver, the wild ox that will not serve at a feeding trough or plow a furrow, and the ostrich. The questions are rhetorical; they press Job to recognize a world full of life that God knows, sustains, and governs, though Job does not (compare Psalm 104:24; Job 12:7–10). The ostrich passage describes a bird that leaves its eggs on the ground and seems careless of its young, yet outruns horse and rider; the text says God has not given her wisdom, and it presents this as part of the strange variety of creation rather than a moral lesson about the bird. The opening line about her wings is difficult in Hebrew and is rendered in different ways. Arminian and Reformed readers generally share the main point: God’s wisdom and care extend to creatures no human governs, and Job is invited to trust a Creator whose ways exceed his understanding.

verses.text: “Do you know the time when the mountain goats give birth? Do you watch when the doe bears fawns?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD asking whether Job knows when mountain goats and does give birth. God attends to lives no human sees.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see detailed providence over the hidden rhythms of creation. Readers in both traditions commonly read the question as humbling Job while revealing God’s care.

verses.text: Can you count the months that they fulfill? Or do you know the time when they give birth?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD asking whether Job can count the months of their pregnancy. God knows the timing of every birth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s knowledge extending to every creature’s life cycle (compare Psalm 104:27). Both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about God’s knowledge and care.

verses.text: They bow themselves. They bear their young. They end their labor pains.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the animals bowing, bearing their young, and ending their labor without human help. Creation follows the order God gave it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sustaining hand in natural processes. Readers in both traditions commonly see the verse as a picture of God’s quiet, constant providence.

verses.text: Their young ones become strong. They grow up in the open field. They go out, and don’t return again.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the young growing strong in the open field and going out never to return. Life moves on under God’s care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see creatures flourishing apart from human oversight. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the LORD’s display of a world Job does not govern.

verses.text: “Who has set the wild donkey free? Or who has loosened the bonds of the swift donkey,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD asking who set the wild donkey free. Freedom in creation is God’s gift and part of his design.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God as the one who assigns each creature its place and nature. Readers in both traditions commonly read the question as pointing Job to the Creator.

verses.text: whose home I have made the wilderness, and the salt land his dwelling place?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see God making the wilderness and the salt land the wild donkey’s home. Even barren places are part of his design.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s purposeful ordering of creatures and habitats. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing God’s care in places humans avoid.

verses.text: He scorns the tumult of the city, neither does he hear the shouting of the driver.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the wild donkey scorning the noise of the city and the shouting of the driver. Not every creature is meant for human service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the limits of human dominion in a world God governs. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as humbling human assumptions of control.

verses.text: The range of the mountains is his pasture. He searches after every green thing.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the mountains as the wild donkey’s pasture as it searches for every green thing. God provides for it in the wild.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s provision for creatures beyond human reach (compare Psalm 104:14). Both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about God’s care.

verses.text: “Will the wild ox be content to serve you? Or will he stay by your feeding trough?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD asking whether the wild ox will serve Job or stay by his trough. Some creatures refuse domestication.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the wild ox as a picture of strength beyond human command. Readers in both traditions commonly read the question as exposing the limits of Job’s power.

verses.text: Can you hold the wild ox in the furrow with his harness? Or will he till the valleys after you?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD asking whether Job can harness the wild ox to plow his valleys. Human control has its limits.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the contrast between God’s rule and human weakness. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the LORD’s gentle but firm humbling of Job.

verses.text: Will you trust him, because his strength is great? Or will you leave to him your labor?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD asking whether Job would trust the wild ox’s great strength with his labor. Strength is not the same as reliability.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the folly of trusting what one cannot govern. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as pointing to trust in God rather than in creatures.

verses.text: Will you confide in him, that he will bring home your seed, and gather the grain of your threshing floor?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD asking whether Job could rely on the wild ox to bring in his harvest. The animal answers to God, not to Job.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the creature’s independence as a reminder of God’s sole sovereignty over creation. Both traditions commonly read the verse within the speech’s wider point.

verses.text: “The wings of the ostrich wave proudly, but are they the feathers and plumage of love?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD turning to the ostrich, whose wings wave proudly. The variety of creation includes the surprising and unusual.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the ostrich as part of God’s diverse handiwork. Readers in both traditions commonly read the description as the text gives it, without mockery of the creature.

verses.text: For she leaves her eggs on the earth, warms them in the dust,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the ostrich leaving her eggs on the earth to warm in the dust. Her ways differ from those of other birds.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a creature whose habits seem strange to human observers. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the LORD’s portrait of a world beyond Job’s understanding.

verses.text: and forgets that the foot may crush them, or that the wild animal may trample them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the ostrich forgetting that a foot or a wild animal may crush her eggs. Her life is marked by apparent carelessness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the creature’s vulnerability described plainly. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as description rather than a lesson about the bird’s worth.

verses.text: She deals harshly with her young ones, as if they were not hers. Though her labor is in vain, she is without fear,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the ostrich dealing harshly with her young yet remaining without fear. Her nature is unlike what Job might expect.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see creation’s variety, including features that puzzle human observers. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the LORD’s display of creation’s strangeness.

verses.text: because God has deprived her of wisdom, neither has he imparted to her understanding.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the text saying God has not given the ostrich wisdom or understanding. Each creature has the nature God assigned it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God as the one who distributes gifts to each creature as he wills. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as describing the bird’s nature, not judging it.

verses.text: When she lifts up herself on high, she scorns the horse and his rider.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the ostrich lifting herself up and scorning the horse and its rider with her speed. What she lacks in one gift she has in another.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the surprising balance of strengths in creation. Both traditions commonly read the verse as celebrating the remarkable variety of God’s works.
